name: Internet Research Agency

summary.text: The Internet Research Agency (IRA) was a company based in St. Petersburg, Russia. On February 16, 2018, a federal grand jury in the District of Columbia indicted the IRA, two related entities and thirteen Russian nationals, alleging a conspiracy to interfere in U.S. elections by creating social media accounts that appeared to be run by Americans; the indictment alleged that Yevgeniy Prigozhin funded the operation through Concord Management and Consulting. In October 2019 the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's bipartisan report, Volume 2, found that the IRA sought to influence the 2016 election at the direction of the Kremlin, supporting Donald Trump and harming Hillary Clinton's chances, and that its activity continued and increased after the election.

facts.claim: On February 16, 2018, a federal grand jury in the District of Columbia returned an indictment in United States v. Internet Research Agency et al. (No. 1:18-cr-32) charging thirteen Russian nationals and three Russian entities with conspiring to interfere in U.S. elections and political processes. The Department of Justice said twelve of the individuals worked at various times for the Internet Research Agency, a company based in St. Petersburg.
facts.quote: Twelve of the individual defendants worked at various points for the Internet Research Agency, a company based in St. Petersburg.

sources.title: Grand Jury Indicts Thirteen Russian Individuals and Three Russian Companies for Scheme to Interfere in the United States Political System

facts.claim: The indictment alleged that Yevgeniy Prigozhin, a Russian national who controlled Concord Management and Consulting LLC and Concord Catering, funded the conspiracy and approved and supported the IRA's operations. The Special Counsel's 2019 report states that Concord and Prigozhin funded the IRA until at least February 2018. An indictment is an allegation.
facts.quote: PRIGOZHIN approved and supported the ORGANIZATION's operations

facts.claim: All defendants were charged with conspiracy to defraud the United States; the indictment also charged conspiracy to commit wire fraud and bank fraud and aggravated identity theft against the IRA and certain individuals. The conspiracy theory alleged obstruction of the lawful functions of the Federal Election Commission, the Department of Justice and the State Department in administering foreign-involvement disclosure requirements.
facts.quote: the defendants conspired to impair and obstruct those agencies' lawful functions in administering federal foreign-involvement disclosure requirements.

facts.claim: The Department of Justice stated that the indictment did not allege that any American knowingly participated in the charged conduct, nor that the conduct changed the outcome of the 2016 election.
facts.quote: The indictment does not allege that any American knowingly participated, nor that the charged conduct changed the outcome of the 2016 election.

sources.title: Grand Jury Indicts Thirteen Russian Individuals and Three Russian Companies for Scheme to Interfere in the United States Political System

facts.claim: The indictment described the IRA creating social media accounts and pages that appeared to be operated by Americans, including pages named "Secured Borders," "Blacktivist," "United Muslims of America," "Army of Jesus," "South United" and "Heart of Texas."
facts.quote: Those pages included "Secured Borders," "Blacktivist" (to promote the Black Lives Matter movement), "United Muslims of America," "Army of Jesus," "South United" and "Heart of Texas."

sources.title: Internet Research Agency indictment: What the Russians did and how they did it
Indictment, United States v. Internet Research Agency LLC et al., No. 1:18-cr-32 (D.D.C.)

facts.claim: The IRA-run "Heart of Texas" page promoted a "Stop Islamization of Texas" protest outside the Islamic Da'wah Center in downtown Houston at noon on May 21, 2016, while a second Russian-run page, "Save Islamic Knowledge," organized a larger counterprotest at the same place and time; ads targeted at each side did not mention the other event.
facts.quote: "Heart of Texas," a page that posed as a pro-Texas secession organization, promoted a "Stop Islamization of Texas" protest at the opening of a library at an Islamic Center on May 21, 2016. ... A group called "Save Islamic Knowledge" had set up the much larger counterprotest. Ads targeted to each side made no mention of a counterprotest.

sources.title: A Houston protest, organized by Russian trolls
Russian trolls orchestrated 2016 clash at Houston Islamic center, new Senate intel report recalls

facts.claim: The Senate Intelligence Committee's Volume 2 report, released October 8, 2019, found that the IRA sought to influence the 2016 U.S. presidential election by harming Hillary Clinton's chances and supporting Donald Trump at the direction of the Kremlin, and that IRA social media activity was overtly and almost invariably supportive of then-candidate Trump.
facts.quote: The Committee found that the IRA sought to influence the 2016 U.S. presidential election by harming Hillary Clinton's chances of success and supporting Donald Trump at the direction of the Kremlin.

facts.claim: The Senate report found that the IRA's operational focus was predominantly on socially divisive issues such as race, immigration and Second Amendment rights, that it targeted African-Americans more than any other group, and that IRA-associated accounts increased activity after the election across Instagram (238 percent), Facebook (59 percent), Twitter (52 percent) and YouTube (84 percent).
facts.quote: IRA-associated accounts showed a significant spike in activity after the election, increasing across Instagram (238 percent), Facebook (59 percent), Twitter (52 percent), and YouTube (84 percent).

facts.claim: The IRA-operated Facebook page "Army of Jesus" gained about 216,000 followers; on October 19, 2016 it posted a meme depicting Satan and Jesus arm wrestling, which was among the Russian-bought ads released by the House Intelligence Committee.
facts.quote: IRA operatives created an "Army of Jesus" Facebook page, which eventually gained 216,000 followers.

facts.claim: Facebook has said that Internet Research Agency content was served to as many as 150 million people on Facebook and Instagram.
facts.quote: Facebook has said that the Internet Research Agency's content was served to as many as 150 million people on its platforms, including both Facebook and Instagram.

openQuestions: Sources differ on how many individual defendants faced the wire/bank fraud and identity theft counts; check the indictment's counts directly.
The 2016 Houston protest details come from the Houston Chronicle and Dallas Morning News reporting on the indictment and Senate report; the page-level passage in Volume 2 was not quoted.
The Senate report findings are treated as official inquiry findings (status court); the owner may prefer documented.
